name: Warren Buffett
role: Investor, chairman and CEO of Berkshire Hathaway; philanthropist
summary: Buffett is a businessman who speaks publicly on economic policy more than on social or foreign questions. He praises the market system while favouring higher taxes on the very rich, an estate tax, an expanded Earned Income Tax Credit and safety nets, and opposes a large minimum-wage increase. He argues for balanced trade over persistent deficits and has called climate risk worth acting on early.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: On CNN in 2012 he said capitalism overshoots and produces bubbles but 'in the end, we keep finding ways to unleash more human potential', and that 'we haven't lost the secret sauce'.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: His 2015 letter says 'nothing rivals the market system' in delivering what people want and his 2016 letter credits the market system with 'abundance beyond any dreams of our forefathers'.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: His 2010 pledge letter says 'a vast collection of possessions ends up possessing its owner' and that owning half a dozen homes would be a burden.

corporate-influence.rationale: In 2001 he said campaign money buys access and influence in Washington and that this 'will continue unless we do something about it'; his 2004 letter describes CEOs who 'muscled Congress' over option accounting.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: His 2015 letter calls for 'a variety of safety nets' for people whose skills the market values little and says prosperity should not mean penury for the unfortunate; he did not address dependency arguments.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: He states that trade is enormously beneficial and the more the better, which contradicts a bloc shut off from outside trade.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: His 2013 essay treats the exclusion of women from the vote and public office as discrimination to be dismantled, and in 2015 he said a law letting people discriminate by sexual orientation is wrong and should be changed; his 2001 letter says Berkshire does not weigh religion, gender, race or orientation in hiring.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: His 2015 letter calls a cyber, biological, nuclear or chemical attack the major threat citizens face, and in 2026 he called nuclear weapons 'the problem' and said one way or another the US should deal with Iran's enriched uranium.

flat-income-tax.rationale: His 2011 op-ed proposes leaving rates unchanged for 99.7 percent of taxpayers and raising them above $1 million and again above $10 million, a graduated schedule rather than one rate.

free-trade.rationale: 2004 letter: 'true trade' is 'enormously beneficial for both us and them... the more of this, the better', agreeing with Adam Smith. He objects to persistent one-way deficits and in 2025 said balanced trade is good, so his support is qualified.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: On CNN in 2015 he said that if people can exercise discrimination based on sexual orientation, 'that is wrong' and 'somebody better do something about it'.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: He personally favours a 'reformed and expanded Earned Income Tax Credit' (2015 letter) and argued in his WSJ op-ed that it rewards work without distorting markets.

limit-population.rationale: Nulled: the only source was Wikipedia, which reports concern about population growth but no stated policy position.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: 2015 letter: 'Nothing rivals the market system in producing what people want'; he also endorses safety nets and regulated utilities, so not an absolute view.

night-watchman-state.rationale: He advocates safety nets, an expanded EITC, estate tax and higher taxes on the rich, which goes beyond a limited state; he did not address the doctrine by name.

no-bailouts.rationale: His 2008 letter says 'strong and immediate action by government was essential' to avoid a total breakdown, and in his 2010 FCIC interview he called the economy's prospects with no exceptional government assistance 'a disaster'.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: His 2010 Giving Pledge letter says to 'keep all we can conceivably need and distribute the rest to society' and asks hundreds of rich Americans to pledge at least half their wealth.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: His 2013 essay says male supremacy was written into the Constitution and that women were pushed to the sidelines, while 'the structural barriers for women are falling' now; at Fortune's 2013 summit he said half the country's talent was compressed into a few occupations.

precautionary-principle.rationale: 2015 letter: it would be foolish to demand 100% proof of climate damage if prompt action had even a small chance of thwarting it ('Noah's Law'). He framed it for individuals and insurers, not as a statement on regulation specifically.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: On CNN in 2015 he said he would like everyone to make $20 an hour but that raising the minimum to $20 would leave millions unemployed, and his 2015 Wall Street Journal op-ed, as reported by Fortune, said a $15 minimum would reduce employment.

reduce-immigration.rationale: On ABC in 2013 he asked for a more logical immigration policy that would 'attract a lot of people', tens or hundreds of thousands of skilled ones, and said the reform should offer undocumented immigrants the chance to become citizens.

social-market-economy.rationale: He pairs strong praise of the market system with safety nets and an expanded EITC, and approves fair regulation of utilities.

state-harmful.rationale: He calls for government action and approves government rescue in 2008 and regulated utilities; no direct statement on the state's necessity.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: His 2003 Fortune plan for import certificates is, in his words, a tariff 'neither protecting specific industries nor punishing specific countries', and in 2025 he said trade should not be used as a weapon.

tax-inheritance.rationale: He testified to the Senate that a meaningful estate tax is needed and opposed repeal; he did not say how heavy it should be.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: In his 2011 New York Times op-ed he asked Congress to raise rates on income above $1 million, with a further increase above $10 million, and on CNN in 2010 he said 'we should raise taxes on the very rich'.

taxation-theft.rationale: He repeatedly argues the rich should pay more tax and says Berkshire expects and ought to pay much more; this is incompatible with calling taxation theft, though he never addressed the claim directly.

trade-surplus.rationale: 2004 letter: a $0.6 trillion US surplus would be 'mercantilism – a long-discredited economic strategy' that he 'would condemn'; he sought balanced trade rather than surpluses.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Nulled: the only source was Wikipedia, and it reports support for wider coverage, not for the government providing universal healthcare.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: He said a meaningful estate tax is needed 'to prevent our democracy from becoming a dynastic plutocracy' and called dynastic wealth contrary to what built the country.

women-suffrage.rationale: His 2013 essay presents the 19th Amendment's vote for women as a correction of discrimination and calls the ethical case for removing the remaining barriers compelling.

notes: Positions come from the Berkshire letters (2001-2016), his own op-eds and essays (New York Times 2011, Fortune 2003 and 2013, the Giving Pledge letter), CNN interviews in the MediaSum corpus and two recent transcripts. He speaks on tax, trade, women's equality, discrimination and the 2008 rescue, and says almost nothing on religion, nationalism, secession, race, war, civil liberties or constitutional structure; those lines stay unreached, so he fails the uncertainty rule. Themes searched with no result: religion and the state, guns, Iraq, Social Security, the death penalty, drugs, Dodd-Frank, climate policy, unions, healthcare policy. His foundation's grants and his endorsements of candidates are not treated as positions. The 2012 New York Times and 2015 Wall Street Journal op-eds could not be opened and are cited through reports or his later interviews. The earlier pass cited Wikipedia for two answers (healthcare, population); this pass nulled them, and replaced the Reuters report of his 2011 op-ed with the op-ed itself.

booksNotUsed.reason: A search of the Project Gutenberg catalog for Buffett found no work by him; his own texts are the Berkshire letters and the op-eds and essays cited.
